The faunal assemblages from the Baxian and Naxian caves are taxonomically diverse and remarkably similar in composition (Supplementary Information 3 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Both assemblages include numerous taxa that have since become locally extinct, including Pongo, Elephas and rhinoceros Dicerorhinus, though most remain extant elsewhere in Asia. Notably, H. erectus, Stegodon and ‘Megalovis’ are globally extinct. Habitat preference analysis indicates that both assemblages are strongly dominated by forest-dwelling taxa (Supplementary Fig. 3), which is consistent with predominantly forested landscapes during the time of deposition.

The plant-equivalent stable carbon isotope values for the Baxian faunal teeth, after correction for species-specific diet-to-enamel enrichment factors based on body mass29 (Supplementary Information 9), range from −31.5 to −23.0‰ (average = −27.6 ± 1.87‰ (1σ)), while lower values observed at the Naxian cave range from −34.0 to −25.1‰ (average = −29.4 ± 2.45‰ (1σ)). Both assemblages yield values well below the dense-canopy forest threshold of −27.5‰ (ref. 28), with no evidence of C4 plant consumption or even C3–C4 intermediate signatures (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 9). These data indicate that the fauna at both sites derived their dietary carbon exclusively from C3 vegetation, with the frequency of canopy-related values exceeding those reported for equatorial African rainforest systems29 and being comparable to that documented for western Amazonian forests30,31,32. This pattern is particularly notable given that several of the taxa represented in the assemblages are known elsewhere to exploit mixed C3–C4 resources or to incorporate substantial C4-derived inputs into their diets in more open environments16.

In a recent development, independent oxygen isotope (δ18O) and clumped isotope (Δ47) analyses further support these environmental reconstructions, indicating humid tropical conditions with higher precipitation and cooler temperatures than modern values in this region (Extended Data Fig. 9 and Supplementary Information 9 and 10).

It has been revealed that three H. erectus teeth from the Naxian cave (NX-B1, NX-B2 and NX-A1) show similarly low isotopic values, with carbon values ranging from −15.0 to −14.0‰, which fall at the boundary between dense-canopy forest and more open C3 vegetation. Although the dataset is limited (n = 3) and at the moment restricted to the Naxian locality, these values are fully consistent with those observed across the much larger faunal assemblage and fall within the range expected for consumers deriving their dietary carbon from closed-canopy C3 vegetation, demonstrating that these late H. erectus populations exploited tropical rainforest resources.

Industry observers note that high-resolution trace element mapping on one H. erectus individual from the Baxian cave (PA1799) yielded 87Sr/86Sr ratios ranging from 0.7110 to 0.7220 (Supplementary Information 11 and Extended Data Fig. 10), while three H. erectus teeth sampled from the Naxian cave revealed overlapping but distinct ranges. All four individuals indicate either movement between geologically distinct regions or consumption of resources from multiple locations during childhood (2–6 years), corresponding to the period of tooth formation.

Sources indicate that A regional strontium isoscape for southern China and northern Southeast Asia33 (Supplementary Information 11) reveals substantial spatial heterogeneity in predicted 87Sr/86Sr ratios, with the local Baxian–Naxian region characterized by relatively homogeneous values (0.710–0.715), reflecting the dominant Carboniferous–Permian limestone karst geology (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 10). More radiogenic signatures (0.717–0.723) occur to the west and northwest in mountainous areas underlain by Precambrian and Palaeozoic metamorphic rocks, while intermediate to more radiogenic values (0.715–0.720) characterize regions to the south, including the Red River valley of northern Vietnam.

Industry observers note that geographic assignment probability maps generated for three representative 87Sr/86Sr values observed in the human tooth profiles indicate that these H. erectus individuals may have moved between the local limestone karst regions and more distant areas during childhood, with the most radiogenic signatures potentially pointing towards areas as far afield as northern Vietnam, which connect southern China with mainland Southeast Asia (Figs. 1 and 3 and Extended Data Fig. 10).

Our results demonstrate that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 8), representing, to our knowledge, the youngest reliably dated occurrence of this species in China and the first with robust chronological constraints from southern China. The integration of multiple independent dating techniques combined with Bayesian age modelling provides unprecedented temporal resolution for late H. erectus in mainland Asia. These findings fundamentally alter our understanding of the species’ persistence and distribution in China, extending the documented record by more than 200,000 years beyond the previous youngest occurrences in Hexian and Nanjing14,15, and establishing southern China as a key region for late-surviving populations during the late Middle Pleistocene (for example, ref. 19).

The temporal importance of this discovery extends beyond simply filling a chronological gap. The age uncertainty range of 324–184 ka places these H. erectus populations at some point within marine isotope stages 9 through 6, raising intriguing questions about potential contemporaneity or overlap with Homo longi (Denisovans) identified in Cobra cave (Laos)34, Baishiya cave (Tibetan Plateau)35, Harbin (northeast China)36,37,38 and the Penghu Channel off the western shore of Taiwan39. The temporal proximity of these various hominin populations across China during the late Middle Pleistocene suggests a more complex biogeographical landscape than previously recognized, with multiple hominin lineages potentially coexisting across different ecological zones and elevational gradients.

Recent findings suggest that moreover, the environmental context revealed by our multi-proxy analyses challenges prevailing assumptions about late H. erectus ecological constraints and mobility patterns. The combined evidence demonstrates unequivocally that these late H. erectus populations exploited closed-canopy tropical rainforest environments and may have conducted long-distance movement beyond the local karst terrain during childhood. The ecological implications of this rainforest use and mobility are profound. Archaeological evidence has so far suggested that H. sapiens was the only member of our genus to specialize in the regular exploitation of these environments18, as early as 150 ka in western Africa40,41. In Southeast Asia, recent isotopic observations of declines in C4 environments and expansion of rainforest in the Middle to early Late Pleistocene have been associated with the disappearance of non-H. sapiens hominin taxa42,43, seemingly unable to shift from mixed savannah–woodland habitats to these increasingly closed forests16,44. However, our data directly challenge this view by demonstrating that H. erectus was not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments (Fig. 3) and that long-distance mobility into these environments may have been a common behavioural pattern rather than exceptional behaviour by isolated individuals.

These findings contrast markedly with Early and Middle Pleistocene H. erectus occupations at Trinil3 and Sangiran in Java4 (Extended Data Fig. 9b). The youngest Javanese H. erectus at Ngandong2 persisted in relatively open woodland refugia2, leading to suggestions that expanding rainforests may have contributed to the species’ eventual extinction in Java2,16. Among early hominin-bearing sites in East and Southeast Asia (Extended Data Fig. 9b), the Naxian and Baxian cave results most closely resemble those from Lida Ajer, Sumatra (73–63 ka), an early H. sapiens site also characterized by closed-canopy rainforest45. This demonstrates that H. erectus was, at minimum, capable of persisting among rainforest fauna, even if such habitats did not represent its optimal ecological niche.

Recent findings suggest that areas in northern Vietnam, such as the Red River valley (Figs. 1 and 3), have long been recognized as a critical biogeographical corridor connecting the karst uplands of southern China with the lowlands of mainland Southeast Asia24. The limited strontium isotope evidence tentatively suggests that late H. erectus populations may have been utilizing similar corridors for seasonal movements, long-distance migrations or resource procurement. This large range (potentially around 250 km) through mostly enclosed environments challenges assumptions about the limited ranging behaviour of H. erectus and suggests behavioural sophistication in landscape use.

According to recent reports, our findings collectively demonstrate that late Middle Pleistocene H. erectus was present in southern China, surviving contemporaneously with H. longi and exhibiting considerable ecological and behavioural flexibility. Rather than being restricted to open savanna or woodland habitats, as traditionally assumed, these populations persisted in closed-canopy tropical rainforests while simultaneously engaging in potential long-distance mobility across diverse ecological and geological landscapes. This evidence challenges the characterization of H. erectus as a species unable to exploit complex tropical forest environments. Whether these adaptations were specific to the late-surviving populations in southern China alone remains to be seen, but further stable isotope work on other Middle Pleistocene sites is vital to address this question. However, the presence of morphologically and genetically confirmed H. erectus in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, combined with the environmental and suggested mobility evidence, is sufficient to necessitate a re-evaluation of the species’ adaptive capabilities, biogeographical range and ultimate fate in mainland Asia.

The caves were discovered using local knowledge and targeted reconnaissance hunting for breccia in the rear chambers. The locations of test pits within the caves were selected on the basis of these reconnaissance surveys. Excavation grids were based on the shape of cave passages and distribution of fossil-rich deposits. Jackhammers were used to break blocks of fossil breccia, and the fossils were extracted using geological hammers. Fine cleaning, identification and cataloguing were conducted in the laboratories at Shandong University and the Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Palaeoanthropology (IVPP).

The fossil-bearing breccia and associated sediments from the fossil chambers of both caves were sampled in situ under subdued red-light conditions (Fig. 2a,d) and were processed using standard sample purification procedures for quartz and feldspar separation including a 40% and 10% wash in hydrofluoric acid for 45 and 10 mins, respectively46. Single aliquots of 90–125 µm feldspar and 180–212 µm quartz or feldspar grains were processed in a Riso TL-DA-20 equipped with an automated DASH set-up, a dual-laser single-grain attachment47 and a blue- and ultraviolet-sensitive Electron Tube photo-multiplier tube (PDM9107Q-AP-TTL-03), using either a blue filter pack (Schott BG-39, 2 mm, and Corning 7-59, 4 mm) for feldspars or U340 filters (2 × Hoya U340, 3.5 mm) for quartz. Data were collected using Sequence Pro v.4.65 and analysed in Analyst v.4.57, DRAC v.1.3 and on spreadsheets designed in Microsoft Excel 365 v.2607. Feldspar equivalent doses were corrected according to the results of the anomalous fading tests (using a weighted mean fading rate of 2.0 ± 0.2% per decade)48, but no residual corrections were undertaken, and the equivalent doses for both feldspar and quartz were then run through either a central age model for the single-aliquot results or a minimum age model49 to identify the single-grain population that experienced the most bleaching before burial. All luminescence analysis was conducted at the ‘Traps’ luminescence dating facility at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia.

Measurements of 238U, 235U, 232Th and 40K were estimated using Geiger–Muller multi-counter beta counting and thick-source alpha counting of dried and powdered sediment samples in the laboratory, combined with in situ gamma spectrometry in the field. The corresponding (dry) beta and gamma dose rates were obtained using the conversion factors in ref. 50 and the beta-dose attenuation factors in ref. 51. Cosmic-ray dose rates were estimated from previously published relationships52, making allowance for the sediment overburden at the sample locality (ranging from 3.99 to 0.20 m), the altitude (ranging from 2,000 to 176 m above sea level) and geomagnetic latitude and longitude of the sampling sites.

Seven H. erectus teeth from the Naxian (n = 6) and Baxian (n = 1) caves were analysed for U-series dating across two laboratories in China and Australia. U-series measurements were undertaken using a laser-ablation multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (MC-ICP-MS) at the Geoarchaeology and Archaeometry Research Group (GARG), Southern Cross University, according to protocols in ref. 53 and in a Neptune MC-ICP-MS at the School of Geography Science, Nanjing Normal University according to refs. 54,55. Laser ablation (at Southern Cross University) was performed with a Upcoming Wave Research 213 nm laser, and thorium (230Th, 232Th) and uranium (234U, 235U, 238U) isotopes were measured on a Thermo Neptune XT MC-ICP-MS. Teeth were ablated using rasters of 5 min each and were measured with standards before and after. Uranium and thorium were separated using conventional anion-exchange chromatography at Nanjing, and the U–Th solution was then introduced into the MC-ICP-MS via a DSN-100 desolvation nebulizer system. Isotopic ratios were measured using a detector configuration that allows for the simultaneous measurement of U and Th isotopes56,57.

Industry observers note that one H. erectus tooth and one Pongo tooth from the Baxian cave (n = 2) were selected for coupled ESR and U-series dating at GARG, Southern Cross University. Enamel fragments from each tooth were separated using a hand-held diamond saw following the protocol developed in ref. 58. Fragments were then measured at room temperature on a Freiberg MS5000 ESR X-band spectrometer at a modulation amplitude of 0.1 mT, 10 scans, 2 mW power, 100 G sweep and 100 kHz modulation frequency. Each fragment was irradiated, following exponentially increasing irradiation times. Sediment elemental concentrations, external beta and gamma dose rate contributions, and water content were obtained from in situ measurements. The external beta-dose rates have been extrapolated from the U, Th and K contents measured on a portion of sediment sub-sample (approximately 8 g). The external gamma dose rates were determined in situ using a portable gamma spectrometer at each site. The equivalent doses were estimated using Matlab-based MCdose software v.2.0.

According to recent reports, separate sub-samples were hand-drilled from the fresh cross-section of the in situ capping flowstones from Naxian and Baxian caves and processed at the Radiogenic Isotope Facility, University of Queensland (n = 6), and six soda straws and one sample of secondary calcite cement were processed at the School of Geography Science, Nanjing Normal University (n = 7). The powdered sub-samples were subjected to chemical treatment and isotopic measurements by mass spectrometry56. U-series dating of the speleothem samples were conducted at the University of Queensland using a Nu Plasma MC-ICP-MS, and analytical procedures followed previous publications for MC-ICP-MS57,58,59. The 230Th/234U ages were calculated using Isoplot EX 3.75 (ref. 60) and half-lives of 75,690 years for 230Th and 245,250 years for 234U (ref. 61). U-series dating of the speleothem samples was carried out at Nanjing Normal University using a Neptune MC-ICP-MS. U-series ages were calculated using the half-lives of 75,584 years for 230Th and 245,620 years for 234U (ref. 62). Non-radiogenic 230Th was corrected using an assumed bulk-Earth atomic 230Th/232Th ratio of (4.4 ± 2.2) × 10−6 (refs. 54,55).

According to recent reports, two Bayesian modelling programs were used to analyse selected independent age estimates (n = 43) (Supplementary Information 8) and to evaluate the uncertainties associated with the combined dating techniques applied to both sites (Supplementary Tables 7–15): OxCal (v.4.4.4, available at https://c14.arch.ox.ac.uk/oxcal.html)63 and ChronoModel (v.3.2.7, https://chronomodel.com/)64. The analyses incorporated the probability distributions of individual ages, constraints imposed by stratigraphic relationships and the reported minimum or maximum nature of some of the individual age estimates. Each individual age was included as a Gaussian distribution (with mean and s.d. defined by the age estimate and their associated uncertainties), and the resulting age ranges for each phase of deposition were presented at 2σ. OxCal allows the identification of boundary ages between each layer to constrain the fossil layer and ChronoModel was applied to assess the extent to which identical or similar data could be obtained. Both modelling results have been presented for transparency.

Three H. erectus specimens from the Naxian cave, as well as 47 faunal teeth from the Baxian cave and 38 from the Naxian cave (n = 41 in total), were taxonomically identified and prepared for stable isotope analysis, following established preparation methods65 (but see refs. 66,67). The resulting δ13C and δ18O values were measured using a ThermoFisher MAT253+ in six separate measurement blocks per sample at the Earth and Environmental Sciences’ Stable Isotope Geochemistry Laboratory at the University of Queensland. The evolved CO2 gases from the Naxian teeth were analysed for carbon and oxygen isotope compositions using a Thermo Delta V Advantage isotope ratio mass spectrometer housed at the Key Laboratory of Archaeological Sciences and Technology, Shandong University. Stable isotope measurements on the three H. erectus teeth were carried out at the Service de spectrométrie de masse isotopique du Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle, Paris, and analysed using a Thermo Delta V Advantage isotope ratio mass spectrometer. To assess isotopic differences among sites, we applied non-parametric and multivariate tests. For univariate comparisons, Kruskal–Wallis tests revealed highly significant differences in both δ13Ccarbon source (χ² = 181.5, d.f. = 6, P < 0.001) and δ18O (χ² = 114.4, d.f. = 6, P < 0.001) among sites. All statistical analyses were conducted using the open-source program R software (v.4.5.1)68.

In a recent development, three in situ samples were collected in bulk (CBAX2, CBAX3, CBAX4) from the breccia at Baxian and the clumped isotope analysis was undertaken in the Macquarie GeoAnalytical Stable Isotope Facility using a ThermoFisher dual-inlet MAT253+ mass spectrometer. The results were processed using the Easotope software package69. The final Δ47 value for each sample was then averaged and reported with 95% confidence intervals, before temperatures were calculated using the calibration in ref. 70 for 90 °C reactions. Using these temperatures, the oxygen isotopic composition of the precipitating fluid (δ18Ofluid) was calculated using the equation in ref. 71.

In a recent development, one H. erectus tooth from Baxian was sectioned with a high-precision diamond saw and polished to a smoothness of greater than 5 μm. Laser ablation combined with ICP-MS was used for trace elemental mapping analyses using an ESI NWR193 coupled to an Agilent 7900 ICP-MS at GARG, Southern Cross University, according to the procedures in refs. 19,72. A laser spot size of 40 μm, a scan speed of 80 μm s−¹, a laser intensity of 60% (approximately 1 J mm−2) and a total integration time of 0.50 s were used to produce data points that corresponded to a pixel size of approximately 40 × 40 μm. NIST610 and NIST612 (certified standard reference materials) were used to assess signal drift. Strontium isotope analysis (87Sr/86Sr) was conducted on four H. erectus teeth: one from Baxian cave and three from Naxian cave, also using laser-ablation MC-ICP-MS at the GARG facility. Enamel fragments were carefully extracted from regions showing low uranium concentrations and distinct elemental signatures from the surrounding dentine according to the mapping results. To contextualize the 87Sr/86Sr values obtained and assess potential mobility patterns, a regional strontium isoscape was constructed for southern China and northern Southeast Asia. The isoscape modelling was based on random forest ensemble machine learning analyses adapted from the original script developed in ref. 33 and followed the method fully described in ref. 21.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

a-d Naxian cave, a and b the cave – location marked with a red star - is situated on the outer cone of a karst inselberg located close to a highway. c a montage of images to demonstrate the speleology of the cave with the small entrance and flowstone step that leads into the stalagmite chamber dense with speleothem, a larger chamber with narrow and high ceilings and terminating with a small fossil chamber with breccia, d the fossil bearing breccia at the highest point of the cave capped with flowstone and underlain by a younger underlying mixed material below. e-h Baxian Cave e and f the cave is also situated on the outer edge of a karst cone with the limestone corridor than connects both caves, cave location is marked with a red star, g a montage of images to demonstrate the speleology and sedimentology of the cave from the wide and high entrance to the narrower and smaller passage that lead to the confined fossil chamber, h the fossil bearing breccia at the highest point of the cave capped with flowstone and underlain with the younger underlying mixed material. There is a remarkable similarity between the stratigraphy and sedimentology of these deposits and associated fossils (d, h).

a Naxian profile, b Baxian profile illustrating the changing speleology and cave deposits from the upper fossil chambers down to the entrances. Baxian is longer than Naxian but slopes at a lesser angle than the steeper Naxian. Images illustrate the main features found in both caves including a wider chamber and smaller fossil chambers. The images of the fossil chambers are taken from a 3D models of the caves (Supplementary Information 2 for links).

a The diverging bar plots demonstrate the taxonomic compositions of the Baxian and Naxian faunas (b), revealing their remarkable similarity. a: Combined p-value (physical uranium uptake parameter) trajectories for enamel and dentine illustrating the relative goodness-of-fit of uranium-uptake histories over the modelled time interval. The enamel curve indicates a broader temporal sensitivity, while dentine exhibits steeper p-value responses reflecting higher susceptibility to uranium migration. b: Normalised uranium-uptake curves for enamel (red) and dentine (green) showing contrasting U-uptake kinetics, with enamel characterised by delayed uptake and dentine by more rapid early incorporation. c: Frequency distribution of modelled ages generated under the US-ESR age model, illustrating the central tendency and dispersion of the Monte-Carlo age simulations used to derive the final age estimate, d H. erectus tooth from Baxian that was dated using US-ESR techniques (Supplementary Information 6).

Recent findings suggest that a and b are the dating results (n = 43) as separate age estimates in kyr for the five dating techniques modelled according to Oxcal and applied to the sediments and fossils of Naxian (a) and Baxian (b) caves. Data are presented as mean values +/− SD. The techniques are colour coded according to the legend and organised into the unit in which they were sampled from – the flowstone, breccia or underlying clay. Some of the techniques represent minimum ages (such as the US ages on teeth) and contain a colour coded arrow pointing the right, while other represent maximum ages such as the pIR-IRSL single aliquot dating of feldspars and contain a colour coded arrow pointing the left. The thick black horizontal boxes with dashed lines represent the boundary ages (and errors) estimated by the modelling. The boundary ages quoted represent the upper and lower age ranges for the breccia units in both caves. c and d are the dating results (n = 43) as separate age estimates in kyr modelling according to Chronomodel for the same five dating techniques. Data are presented as mean values +/− SD. The individual sample events have been organised into three phases; breccia deposition (including fossil and sediment ages), overlying flowstone precipitation and underlying clay deposition with each phase represented by a different plot. The timescale goes from more recent on the right (50 ka written as -50000) to oldest on the left (400 ka written as -400000). For Baxian (c) we have used the age uncertainty at 2 σ (95%) of the fossil teeth dated using US-ESR (H. erectus and Pongo), resulting in an age of 324-184 ka. For Naxian (d), the fossils are all dated using US only so represent minimum ages, so instead we have used the period between the overlying flowstone (as the minimum age) and the youngest soda straw in the breccia (as the maximum age) both at 2 σ (95%) uncertainty to constrain the age of breccia deposition at 319-241 ka. The use of Chronomodel compared to Oxcal has accentuated similar events and reduced the younger age uncertainty by around 20 kyr. The overlapping uncertainty between the two caves has been used to represent a Homo erectus presence at some point between 324-184 ka.

a Taxon-specific δ13Ccarbon source values in relation to vegetation type. δ13Ccarbon source (plant-equivalent values; ‰ VPDB at Baxian (324-184) and Naxian (319-241 ka). Shaded background areas indicate ecological zones: dense canopy forest (dark green), C3 vegetation (light green), and C4 grassland (yellow). The unshaded interval between C3 and C4 represents the C3–C4 intermediate zone. This framework allows direct comparison of faunal isotopic signatures against expected vegetation regimes. A large proportion of taxa from both sites fall within the dense canopy forest zone, supporting the interpretation of closed-canopy rainforest environments. The H. erectus values (red stars) fall within the C3 forest domain and plot at the boundary between dense canopy forest and more open C3 vegetation. b Vegetation zone proportions at hominin-bearing sites in Southeast Asia and South China. Proportional distribution of faunal δ13Ccarbon source values assigned to vegetation zones (dense canopy C3, open C3, C3–C4 intermediate, and C4). Bars show the relative contributions of each zone across six hominin-bearing sites: Trinil4, Sangiran5, Cobra Cave34,73, Duoi U’Oi74, Lida Ajer45,75, Baxian and Naxian. Baxian and Naxian are dominated by C3 signals, with substantial contributions from dense canopy vegetation, while Trinil and Sangiran show higher proportions of intermediate and C4 values, reflecting more open habitats. Lida Ajer is strongly weighted toward dense canopy values, consistent with closed rainforest settings. Together, these results illustrate marked ecological contrasts between late H. erectus contexts in China and Javanese sites, as well as affinities between Naxian and the rainforest environment of early H. sapiens at Lida Ajer75,76,77.

a Trace element distribution maps of the Baxian H. erectus tooth. LA-ICP-MS elemental maps showing the distribution of (i) 7Li/43Ca, (ii) 88Sr/43Ca, (iii) 138Ba/43Ca, and (iv) 238U/43Ca ratios normalised to calcium across a longitudinal section of the tooth. All maps show both enamel (upper/left portion, blue-green colours) and dentine (lower/right portion, predominantly dark red). The colour scales are optimised to visualise variation within the enamel tissue. Dark red areas in the dentine for Sr, Ba, and U maps indicate significantly elevated concentrations due to post-depositional diagenetic uptake from the burial environment, rendering these tissues unsuitable for life history reconstruction. In contrast, the enamel tissue displays lower concentrations and visible banding patterns, particularly Ba/Ca, and Sr/Ca maps, which reflect biogenic signals. The U/Ca map clearly illustrates the extent of diagenetic alteration, with the highest concentrations in dentine and at the enamel-dentine junction (EDJ), demonstrating the vulnerability of dental tissues to post-depositional elemental exchange. The Li/Ca map highlights elevated concentrations in both tissues with distinct banding in the enamel. All measurements were obtained using LA-ICP-MS with 40 μm spot size and Ca-normalization to account for matrix effects. b Strontium isotope ratio profiles across H. erectus tooth enamel from Baxian and Naxian caves. LA-MC-ICP-MS 87Sr/86Sr ratio profiles measured along linear transects across tooth enamel from (i) BAX-1 from Baxian Cave, and (ii) NX-A1, (iii) NX-B1, and (iv) NX-B2 from Naxian Cave. The x-axis represents distance in mm along the ablation transect from the cervical region toward the cusp, corresponding to the temporal sequence of enamel formation from early to late childhood. The y-axis shows 87Sr/86Sr ratios, with variation reflecting changes in geological substrate accessed through diet and drinking water during tooth formation. All four individuals exhibit substantial intra-tooth variation in 87Sr/86Sr ratios that exceeds analytical uncertainty, indicating mobility between geologically distinct regions or consumption of resources from multiple locations during childhood. BAX-1 shows 87Sr/86Sr ratios ranging from 0.7110 to 0.7220, while the Naxian specimens display overlapping ranges: NX-A1 (0.7115-0.7165), NX-B1 (0.7095-0.7165), and NX-B2 (0.7100-0.7160). The observed variation patterns provide evidence for landscape mobility of late Middle Pleistocene H. erectus populations in southern China. c Strontium isoscape and geographic assignment probabilities for H. erectus mobility in southern China and northern Southeast Asia. (i) Regional-scale strontium isoscape showing predicted bioavailable 87Sr/86Sr ratios across southern China, northern Vietnam, northern Laos, and adjacent regions. Colours indicate 87Sr/86Sr values ranging from 0.710 (dark blue) to 0.725 (pink), with the Baxian/Naxian cave sites marked by a white dot. Major cities (Hanoi, Lào Cai, Guilin) are shown for geographic reference. (ii) Prediction uncertainty map for the regional isoscape, showing standard error of predicted 87Sr/86Sr values ranging from 0.004 (yellow, low uncertainty) to 0.016 (purple, high uncertainty). (iii) Local-scale isoscape focused on a 400 km × 400 km region centred on the Baxian/Naxian sites, with scale bar representing 50 km. (iv) Prediction uncertainty map for the local isoscape (v-vii) Geographic assignment probability maps for three representative 87Sr/86Sr values observed in H. erectus tooth enamel: (v) Seq1 = 0.714, representing average values for NX-A1 and lower values in NX-B2, showing high assignment probabilities (yellow-green) concentrated within 30-50 km of the cave sites in limestone karst terrain; (vi) Seq2 = 0.719, representing transitional values observed in multiple specimens, showing assignment probabilities extending southward ~150-250 km toward the Red River valley region; (vii) Seq3 = 0.724, representing the most radiogenic values observed (particularly in BAX-1), showing assignment probabilities concentrated in the Red River valley foothills approximately 250 km south of the caves and near Lào Cai to the west, with very low probabilities in the local cave area (dark purple). The progressive southward shift in assignment probabilities from Seq1 to Seq3 indicates long-distance mobility of late H. erectus individuals between the local karst uplands and distant regions up to 250 km away during childhood tooth formation. All isoscapes generated using random forest machine learning based on33 global bioavailable strontium database.

McInnes wants a quiet January... but it might just be the right time for Rangers to cash in on Raskin

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (480 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 11:37 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 11:44 EST, 20 November 2026.
  • Derek McInnes can be understood in wanting a quiet January window.
  • In the case of Olwethu Makhanya, for example, this is definitely not the time to sell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 11:37 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 11:44 EST, 20 November 2026.

Derek McInnes can be understood in wanting a quiet January window. He’s still bonding a squad of players together. Drama and diversions are the last thing he needs when there looks to be an opportunity to win a title on the horizon.

In the case of Olwethu Makhanya, for example, this is definitely not the time to sell.

The 22-year-old South African has been impressive at centre-back, but it will take a campaign catching the attention in high-level European football for him to raise his value to Calvin Bassey levels and beyond.

It has been revealed that same goes for the likes of Ryan Naderi. Getting into the Czechia squad and increasing his range of experience makes him a more interesting prospect, but UEFA competition is a platform that ought to increase his premium.

In a recent development, mcInnes, as he did this week, has to say he wants to keep his more prominent talents anyway. It would be strange to appear accepting of the board cashing in on bigger players.

When it comes to Nico Raskin, however, things are different. A buyer for him should have been found in the summer after his World Cup involvement with Belgium.

Rangers midfielder Nico Raskin is an asset who could be sold in the January transfer window.

From the chit-chat around the game, it does not seem unreasonable to think Rangers maybe overvalued him in the initial part of that window and missed the boat in terms of securing a sale.

If he stays for the rest of this season and enters the final year of his contract, though, the money you can ask for naturally reduces. The club might seek to tie him up on a new deal, of course, but his remarks about being ‘mentally ready to leave’ at the start of the season point to the most likely direction of travel.

In a recent development, is he irreplaceable? Not at all. And this is where forward planning should come into the mix.

If there’s someone out there willing to edge anywhere close to the £15m mark for the 25-year-old, they should be getting sounded out now – with a contingency proposal being discussed and worked on in tandem.

Yes, Rangers need to get back to winning silverware, but the need to start raising funds through selling players – and replacing them - at appropriate times is pressing too.

As often mentioned here, they can’t keep spending money the way they have been without considerably more coming back in return.

Recent findings suggest that raskin’s a good player, but his three-and-a-half years at Ibrox have hardly been shaped by his propensity for winning medals, have they? If a realistic fee is there in January, there’s a case to make for it being taken.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Aren’t friendlies supposed to be non-events?
  • There was only one player the vast majority of the crowd wanted to see in the grandiosely named Boyle Sports Cup and, in chronological order from his 60th minute introduction, he received a standing ovation, hit the bar, had a goal disallowed, missed a penalty in a shoot-out and lifted a trophy.
  • Most remarkably – and, certainly, worryingly – of all, he was central to the game being ended early as five young boys, one after the other, breached security and ran to him in the middle of pitch, all of them successfully posing for photos with the Portuguese.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aren’t friendlies supposed to be non-events? Manchester United against Leeds United in Dublin always had the capacity to be lively, but try explaining the half hour that Bruno Fernandes experienced in one breath. It would be impossible.

There was only one player the vast majority of the crowd wanted to see in the grandiosely named Boyle Sports Cup and, in chronological order from his 60th minute introduction, he received a standing ovation, hit the bar, had a goal disallowed, missed a penalty in a shoot-out and lifted a trophy.

Most remarkably – and, certainly, worryingly – of all, he was central to the game being ended early as five young boys, one after the other, breached security and ran to him in the middle of pitch, all of them successfully posing for photos with the Portuguese.

You could say it was harmless fun but it should not have happened and the flummoxed faces that were pulled on the Manchester United bench, as an army in high-visibility jackets stood and watched it all unfold, suggested they took a dim view.

It has been revealed that it was a shame because in that cameo, Fernandes showed he has returned from the World Cup in excellent shape, the tempo of United’s play immediately lifting when he had the ball. It is wrong to make conclusions in the summer, but you are on safe ground to state he will be integral to their ambitions.

Croke Park is a stadium steeped in history and another chapter was penned here, as the capacity crowd made this the highest attended soccer match in Ireland with 82,000 coming through the gates: it is a magnificent venue, one that would be well capable of hosting a Champions League final.

Michael Carrick hopes in years to come that is the stage where his team will be but, right now, it is a case of learning to walk again before they can run and he more than anyone will know how far off that target is, not that it will stop him trying to get there.

Recent findings suggest that the one thing that is obvious about the way United play under him is the first thought from everyone is to go forward promptly. Yes, this was only a friendly, but the ambition to be on the front foot and cause problems was evident from the start.

The team in red had much the better of the opening exchanges, with Diogo Dalot having the first shot that went over but, unlike on July 25, when Mayo beat Kerry here in Gaelic football’s All Ireland final, which went viral, nobody was cheering the sight of a ball clearing the bar.

It was like a home game for United and the majority got what they wanted in the 15th minute when a slick counter-attack ended with Bryan Mbuemo sliding a pass into Joshua Zikzee, who rifled past James Trafford with a first-time finish.

Devastating counterattack! 💥Manchester United break and Joshua Zirkzee is there to finish it off 🤩 pic.twitter.com/y6QHbZMi7n.

Zirkzee is unlikely to be part of Carrick’s squad beyond the transfer window, with interest from clubs in Italy, and it would be disingenuous to suggest his career at Old Trafford has been successful, but his attitude was exemplary and he played as if he was desperate to change his manager’s mind.

There may have been an anticipation that United would stride clear, but this game was also about Leeds, whose summer has been encouraging and whose confidence from staying up last season has evidently enabled them to blossom.

You would be way off the mark if you include them in your conversations about which clubs are going to be relegated next May, and the sense they showed to stay with Daniel Farke has paid off. They have bought some good players, not least goalkeeper James Trafford and Harry Wilson.

According to recent reports, top stop from James Trafford! 🚫The Leeds United keeper has been busy in the first half... pic.twitter.com/VKmxNVKBsA.

Trafford has done the right thing getting away from Manchester City and you could argue that he is already reaping the benefit of playing for a manager who wants him, as he made a fabulous save in the 23rd minute to thwart Mbuemo. It was all part of performance that led to him being named player of the match.

He was involved in the move that brought the Leeds equaliser, too, as his long clearance caused uncertainty and led to Tyler Fletcher being pickpocketed by Dan James and he nudged a pass into Brenden Aaronson, who kept his cool and danced into the area, ignoring Senne Lammens, to finish.

Leeds hit back with their first shot on target! 💥Brenden Aaronson with a cool finish 🥶 pic.twitter.com/5WsSZY41j6.

According to recent reports, it was an entertaining affair, mercifully lacking the bile that would usually bubble away when it is staged in England, and the longer the game advanced, the better Leeds looked. They finished the opening period strongly and came back after the restart, with 10 changes, in the same fettle.

Farke, whose team had shown their ability to score heavily when they pummelled Liverpool 4-2 in Chicago 10 days ago, would have taken plenty of encouragement, but the perfectionist in him would have cursed the opportunities that were squandered early in the second period.

Sources indicate that the misses proved costly as the game meandered and the shoot-out went United’s way, after Wilson and James Justin failed from 12 yards, with Noussair Mazraoui thumping in the decisive kick. It really is never dull.

Whether it will be enough to keep him at Old Trafford for the long run remains to be seen, particularly as interest from Italy persists, but what can’t be doubted is his attitude. He looks sharp.

It has been revealed that good evening and welcome to live coverage of the pre-season friendly between Manchester United and Leeds United at a sold-out Croke Park in Dublin. Last year Leeds played Milan in the Irish capital and drew a crowd of 52,000 but at the GAA citadel, as I think I’m contractually obliged to call it, there will be 83,000 present, a testament to the Premier League’s reach and these two clubs’ popularity in Ireland founded on the exploits of Billy Whelan, Noel Cantwell, Johnny Giles, Roy Keane, Gary Kelly et al. It’s the first club match ever held at the stadium.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a fixture that always stirs the blood and whenever it comes around you can guarantee that there will be reams of stuff about the War of the Roses, clash in styles, Busby and Revie, Bobby and Jack, large swathes of which this author has been guilty of producing. I’ll spare you all that today because while it’s relevant to fans of both clubs, they know it backwards. And it’s a match that has come around a wee bit too frequently in pre-season recently, first in Perth, Western Australia, in 2019 when Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s side beat Marcelo Bielsa’s 4-0, then in 2023 in Oslo when Erik ten Haag’s second or third string defeated Daniel Farke’s threadbare, just relegated squad 2-0 and last year in Stockholm, which ended in a 0-0 draw between two scratch sides.

It has been revealed that this one comes round later in the pre-season schedule than those three so we can expect to see stronger XIs, at least for part of the game. Leeds’ pre-season has gone well: after a 3-2 defeat by Wrexham in Tampa, they have beaten Sunderland in New Jersey, Liverpool in Chicago and RB Leipzig at Elland Road. Manchester United also lost to Wrexham (in Helsinki) then beat Rosenborg in Trondheim, Atlético in Stockholm and drew one apiece with the European champions, PSG, in Gothenburg last time out.

While Leeds will have latest signing James Trafford available and Noah Okafor, who scored twice in Leeds’ first league victory at Old Trafford for 45 years last April, in the squad for the first time after the World Cup, Manchester United have Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford back in training since the start of the week but it seems too soon for them to start but Youri Tielemans is pushing to make his first start.

#140963. Breaking: Liverpool vs Man Utd: Florian Wirtz leaves his mark with stunning creative display as remarkable stat emerges

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (364 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Liverpool vs Man Utd: Florian Wirtz leaves his mark with stunning creative display as remarkable stat emerges

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (364 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Saikat Mandal | 22 Nov 2026 20:04.
  • Florian Wirtz produced a stellar performance as Liverpool registered an emphatic 4-0 victory over Manchester United in Sunday's Premier League clash at Anfield.
  • Dominik Szoboszlai opened the scoring for the Reds after Leny Yoro was sent off in the eighth minute, before Wirtz doubled their advantage in the first half.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Saikat Mandal | 22 Nov 2026 20:04.

Florian Wirtz produced a stellar performance as Liverpool registered an emphatic 4-0 victory over Manchester United in Sunday's Premier League clash at Anfield.

Dominik Szoboszlai opened the scoring for the Reds after Leny Yoro was sent off in the eighth minute, before Wirtz doubled their advantage in the first half.

Liverpool dominated possession after the interval and added two more goals, with Rio Ngumoha making history for the Reds and Victor Munoz also getting on the scoresheet.

While the Reds remain third in the Premier League table, they have closed the gap on second-placed Manchester City to one point and are seven points adrift of leaders Arsenal.

Andoni Iraola is now unbeaten in his seven Premier League matches against the Red Devils, with only legendary Liverpool manager Jurgen Klopp boasting a longer record, having gone eight games without defeat against the same opposition.

The German international came under heavy criticism from Jamie Carragher at the start of the season as he struggled to make an impact.

Wirtz has gradually rediscovered his confidence and delivered a top-class performance against the Red Devils, creating as many as 10 chances.

According to Opta Joe, Wirtz's tally was the highest by any player in a Premier League match since David Silva created 11 chances against West Bromwich Albion in March 2015.

Wirtz has now registered three goals and five assists across all competitions for the Reds this season, and those numbers are expected to rise in the coming months.

While the victory over a struggling Man Utd side reduced to 10 men may not provide a complete picture, there are signs that Liverpool's players are gradually getting to grips with Iraola's demands.

There was greater cohesion and better team chemistry throughout the contest, and the side could become even stronger once Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni and Conor Bradley return from injury.

Wirtz has covered considerable ground in every match, and his work rate has been second to none, but the end product had been missing.

Iraola will hope that Wirtz can build on this performance and help Liverpool reach newly introduced heights as the season progresses.

AC Milan’s negotiating table has remained busy between the summer and winter windows, with a clear emphasis on contracts.

Extending the discussion to the youth teams, a lot of young talents have signed their first pro deals this year too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An injury-time penalty from returning hero Raul Jimenez ensured Wolves came away with a point in their Championship opener after Blackburn had produced a comeback.

Wolves led through Marshall Munetsi’s cool finish on 18 minutes only for Sean McLoughlin’s first Blackburn goal to draw the visitors level on 27 minutes with a well-timed run and header.

Recent findings suggest that the visitors turned the game around on 48 minutes through Andri Gudjohnsen’s close-range strike only for substitute Jimenez to level the game three minutes into injury time from the spot after Ryan Alebiosu handled the ball in the box. Jimenez and his wife marked his return to Molineux by giving 5,000 fans black scarves emblazoned with the words ‘Si Senor’ - a nod to his song - and Jimenez did not disappoint as he rifled in his penalty.

Industry observers note that LATE DRAMA! 😱Raul Jimenez cooly converts from the penalty spot, deep into added time to save a point for Wolves 🔥 pic.twitter.com/5h2lMxcHNU.

Recent findings suggest that cesar Peixoto wants Wolves to play with their heads rather than their hearts after the home side rescued a late point in the first game of the Championship season following relegation. Wolves replaced Rob Edwards with Portuguese coach Peixoto during the summer and he felt his side’s loss of organisation allowed Blackburn to take control of the game.

Peixoto said: “One point is not what we want, we want three points. We lost some organisation in the second half and played more with our hearts and not our heads and brains.

Industry observers note that “We have to keep our mental stability during the 90 minutes because we’re better when we’re organised. We need to play our way with our identity. It’s a lesson for us to understand when we lose organisation it’s more difficult for us and more easy for the opposition.

According to recent reports, “We’re working hard to bring more solutions [into the club] but we need to work hard with the players we have. It’s the first game, there’s a lot to work on and a lot to improve.”.

According to recent reports, tony Mowbray took charge of Blackburn in the league for the first time since returning to the club for a second stint in the dugout. Rovers recorded their lowest league finish since Mowbray’s first stint in charge of the club last term but the Blackburn boss is confident his side have enough to beat the drop and climb up the table this campaign.

Recent findings suggest that mowbray remarked: “Ultimately, it feels like a defeat, it’s a bit disappointing and a bit frustrating. I just felt a lot of decisions were starting to swing their way. It’s harsh to take, I don’t think they deserved a second goal. We asked the players to be brave and we were collectively very strong.

“Everybody has us relegated, probably on the back of finishing 20th last season and losing a couple of our better players and not spending much money, which is a good motivation for the team. We deserved to win the game, we indicated there’s enough quality to give teams problems and I hope there’s help on the way [in the transfer window].”.

The first chance of the season came the way of Blackburn as a cross-field pass found Alebiosu down the right, who floated a ball into the box only for an unmarked Oladipo Afolayan to head wide from eight-yards out.

However, Wolves scored the first goal of the new campaign when Fer Lopez played a defence-splitting through ball into the path of Munetsi, who coolly found the net with a first time effort from the edge of the penalty area.

"A vibrant Molineux rejoices!" 🎉Marshall Munetsi cooly slots home for Wolves to give them the lead on the opening night of the Championship season 🥶 pic.twitter.com/tVHdbNv3Hq.

Blackburn drew level through an unlikely source just nine minutes later as McLoughlin headed in his first-ever goal in English football in more than 150 games when he met Ryoya Morishita’s cross from the right at the near post.

The home side had chances to retake the lead before the break as Lopez curled a shot narrowly over the top from 20-yards while Kieran Trippier teed up Mateus Mane for a chance as the teenager found the top of the net from distance.

Blackburn turned the game on its head minutes after the break as Gudjohnsen turned home Afolayan’s deflected ball in from the right from close range to stun Molineux into silence.

"It's brilliantly worked by Blackburn Rovers!" 💥Andri Guðjohnsen finishes from close range to turn the game around and the visitors the lead 👏 pic.twitter.com/vkKQQezicK.

Peixoto introduced Jimenez from the bench on the hour mark but even the Mexican could not lift Wolves with Blackburn comfortable for long periods as frustration grew in the stands.

However, Alebiosu handled Jackson Tchatchoua’s cross from the left in injury time and the referee awarded a spot kick which allowed Jimenez to mark his Wolves return with an equaliser from 12-yards as he sent Balazs Toth the wrong way.

According to recent reports, “I think it is a really harsh one. He [the referee] has to be sure at such a critical time of the game. And I do not think he can be sure. I think he has almost had a guess that he is in the box. It is such a substantial call.”.

Recent findings suggest that “We see the ref’s position. The fact the ref makes the decision to give the penalty in my opinion, it is a bigger decision to give it then to not. We have got the luxury of the replays and we are still not sure. His whole body is outside the box.”.

In a recent development, “It looks outside the box to me [the penalty incident]. The still picture suggests to me it was outside the box. We can get better and we will have to. We have to be more dominant with the ball at times and be better in attack. We have done a lot of work on that in pre-season. Having been in this league a long time, the power of the dressing room is crucial and any motivation tool you can you use is important. I think we will be fine. You have to enjoy football and love it. I think the boys enjoyed it tonight.”.

“Obviously frustrated. The boys did everything to get the three points but it is gutting in the end. I thought I was outside the box when the ball came in and the decision went against us. They are saying it is in the box and it is frustrating. We dug deep and thought we had it. I cannot fault everyone as we all put in a shift, it was just the final details with the penalty decision. We deserved the three points. If we play like that every week, we will go far in the table.”.

Raul Jimenez reacts after his late penalty saved a point for Wolves against Blackburn 🗣️ pic.twitter.com/aXvVeWw6fc.

“Before the game we were predicting Wolves would be right up there [this season] and we thought it would be a comfortable win. But that was not the case. Blackburn gave a really good account of themselves and had lots of openings. [Cesar] Peixoto will be breathing a massive sigh of relief with that handball.”.

In a recent development, “Wolves got away with one if I am being really honest. In terms of their second-half performance, they did not do anywhere near enough. I thought Blackburn were excellent throughout and deservedly took the lead. It is a huge decision [to give the penalty], but in the end Raul Jimenez steps up to get his side the point. [Cesar Peixoto] will be delighted to get something in the end.”.

When Wolverhampton Wanderers last attacked the Championship under a Portuguese manager newly introduced to English football, it proved a vintage season.

Molineux was under the spell of Nuno Espírito Santo in that 2017-18 campaign, and the major question is whether César Peixoto can lead a repeat nearly a decade later.

Peixoto was a surprise appointment in June, replacing Rob Edwards, and he has been entrusted with the mission of returning Wolves to the Premier League at the first time of asking.

According to recent reports, “I have changed some things with set-pieces and some things in other moments of the game because I want the team to be organised and understand all the different moments within a match. During pre-season we have scored some goals from high pressing, but we will not be able to press high in every moment of every game. The players have to understand the game and recognise what each moment requires. It is vital that we work as a team. When we can press high, we’ll press high. When we need to defend in a mid-block, we will stay organised. When the opposition pushes us deeper, which will sometimes happen, we have to be organised there as well.

“There are a lot of crosses in the Championship, for example, so the team needs to understand what to do in those situations. We want to play our football, be offensive and react strongly when we lose the ball, but we also need to understand the different moments of the game. I think we are at a good level to attack the Championship.”.

I am going to go for Wolves and Middlesbrough as the other two promoted clubs.

The 2026/27 Championship season kicks off at Molineux as Wolves host Blackburn, with the home side hoping to put the bad memories of last season firmly behind them. There are new playoff rules in place for this season, with six places now up for grabs in the play-offs.

Recent findings suggest that wolves are aiming to return to the Premier League at the first attempt, having endured a miserable season in the top flight last year as they finished bottom with just three wins to their name. It has been a summer of change at the club as they chose to change managers. Rob Edwards lost his job in what was a shock move and was replaced by 46-year-old Cesar Peixoto, with this being his first head coaching position outside of his home country Portugal. Back in 2017/18, Wolves won the Championship title led by Peixoto’s compatriot Nuno Espirito Santo.

“I am ready,” Peixoto told Wolves’ club website. “We have worked very hard during pre-season, and I think we have had a great pre-season. All the players have worked very, very hard and they understand what I want from them. I am ready and confident going into the first game. Football is football, whether it is in Portugal or England, but there are different characteristics to the game here. We have watched, observed and analysed the Championship. We did that work before I came to the club, so we know what to expect.

Industry observers note that “It is going to be a tough season with good teams, but we are prepared to fight for the three points game after game and week after week. We know what we want from the team and we know what our major goal is. We’re going to work very hard and fight to achieve that goal.”.

According to recent reports, they have brought in vast experience on the player side in the shape of Kieran Trippier and Raul Jimenez, who is back at Molineux three years after leaving for Fulham. Although they have lost Brazilian midfielder Joao Gomes to Aston Villa, most of their squad has stayed intact as they pursue promotion back to the top flight. It is a special year for the club as they celebrate their 150th anniversary.

Sources indicate that blackburn, led by experienced manager Tony Mowbray, did not enjoy a great season in the Championship last year, finishing down in 20th place and just five points above the relegation zone. 14 years have now passed since Blackburn last played in the top flight.

According to recent reports, “I think it is a tough start,” Mowbray mentioned. “On paper, I would suggest the first couple of games, particularly, jumped out as a tough start. One of the Premier League sides from last season, away from home. They have got a very talented squad, a pretty expensive squad. They have got some very good individual talent. Yet, there is an argument to say they have not won many football matches in the last calendar year. So, what we get, we will have to wait and see.”.

Industry observers note that these sides last met in the FA Cup during the 2024/25 season, with Wolves winning that fourth-round tie 2-0 thanks to goals from Matheus Cunha and Gomes, both of whom are now plying their trade elsewhere. The omens would appear to be on Wolves’ side as they are unbeaten in their last eight league meetings with Blackburn. Both sides progressed to the second round of the League Cup last weekend, with Wolves beating Port Vale 3-0 and Blackburn overcoming Burton Albion 2-1.

Alphadjo Cisse has definitely been the breakout player of the season so far and Ruben Amorim has no intention of dialling down his presence in attack.

Industry observers note that milan had a very clear strategy when they headed into the current season: Goncalo Ramos would be the main man in attack. Instead, however, it’s the underdog Cisse who has been running the show, while the Portuguese striker has been at the bottom in terms of output.

Recent findings suggest that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

As highlighted by Gazzetta dello Sport this morning (see image below), that’s why there cannot be – and likely won’t be – a Milan without Cisse in attack. Ruben Amorim now wants to build the attack around him, as opposed to introducing him every now and then.

Recent findings suggest that the most recent clash, the 2-1 win against Genoa, was a good example of this. Amorim went for a bold formation with Cisse, Ramos, Christian Pulisic, Diego Moreira, Luka Modric and Adrien Rabiot together. A team with a lot of quality and an attacking-minded style.

In a recent development, it was a shape that reminded us of 2009-10, when Milan were guided by another foreign coach: Leonardo. He chose a very attacking-minded side with four attackers and two midfielders, which is something that Amorim almost replicated.

Modric and Rabiot in front of the defence (Pirlo and Ambrosini then) and the fantasy project with Pulisic, Moreira, Cisse, and Ramos, comparable to the Ronaldinho, Pato, Seedorf, and Borriello of the old days.

Despite this, the goals were scored after two mistakes by Genoa (even if Milan’s pressing helped), so the goal is to repeat the experiment against Frosinone and to increase its effectiveness, the experiment should be repeated tomorrow.

In that sense, Cisse will be key as he’s the top scorer: three goals in Europa League and five in Serie A. He has scored with both feet and his head, demonstrating a combination of talent and an eye for goal: characteristics that are very important for a team like Milan.

The average also speaks for itself: eight goals spread across 658 minutes means he scores a goal every 82 minutes. Best of all, his versatility means that he can play as an attacking midfielder, a left-winger, and even as a centre-forward.

Recent findings suggest that at just 20 years and 17 days old, thanks to the fifth goal in his ninth Serie A appearance, Cisse became the second-youngest player to reach the milestone in the first ten games with Milan, at least since 1994-95. Only Pato did it younger, at 18 years and 181 days.

Furthermore, he’s one of only three players born after 2006 (top five leagues) to have scored eight or more goals in all competitions, along with Lamine Yamal (13) and Paris Brunner, who also scored eight.

As the pink newspaper concludes, Ramos has also produced eye-catching numbers, but in this case in a negative sense: 1,191 minutes on the pitch, three goals scored, meaning one goal scored every 398 minutes.
